why: Venn works Laplace's urn problems as counts: 10,000 drawings, how many reports of each kind, how many of them true. That is a natural-frequency tree, so the lens leads with worked examples whose counts are recomputed and drawn. Venn then argues that the method rarely applies to real stories, so his positions get claim cards, his test cases get counterexample cards, and his citations of Hume, Laplace and others link across the library.

lenses.title: §6. Ten thousand reports about a bag with one white ball
lenses.why: Venn's method is literally a frequency tree; counting makes the collapse from 9/10 to 9/1008 visible.
src: Suppose that there is a bag with 1000 balls, only one of which is white, the rest being all black. A ball is drawn at random, and our witness whose veracity is 9/10 reports that the white ball was drawn.

tree.label: drawings
src: say 10,000; that is, suppose that 10,000 balls having been successively drawn out of this bag

children.label: white is drawn
src: In the 10,000 drawings the white ball would come out 10 times

children.label: he says white: right
src: and therefore be rightly asserted 9 times

children.label: he says black: wrong
src: whilst on the one of these occasions on which he goes wrong he has nothing to say but 'black.'

children.label: black is drawn
src: So with the 9990 occasions on which black is drawn

children.label: he says black: right
src: he is right and says black on 8991 of them

children.label: he says white: wrong
src: and is wrong and therefore says white on 999 of them.

answer.label: Share of his 'white' reports that are true
src: his special veracity, as we may term it, for cases of this description, has been reduced from 9/10 to 9/1008.

lenses.title: §7. The same witness, numbered balls
lenses.why: The contrast case: when there are many ways to be wrong, his errors scatter and his veracity survives intact.
src: Suppose that the balls were all numbered, from 1 to 1,000, and the witness knows this fact. A ball is drawn, and he tells me that it was numbered 25, what are the odds that he is right?

children.label: 25 is drawn
src: in 10,000 drawings this ball would be obtained 10 times, and correctly named 9 times.

children.label: he names 25: right
src: in 10,000 drawings this ball would be obtained 10 times, and correctly named 9 times.

children.label: another ball is drawn
src: But on the 9990 occasions on which it was not drawn there would be a difference

children.label: he errs, spread over 999 wrong numbers
src: Hence his 999 errors, instead of all leading him now back again to one spot, will be uniformly spread over as many distinct ways of going wrong.

children.label: …and the wrong number is 25
src: On one only of these occasions, therefore, will he mention 25 as having been drawn.

answer.label: Share of his '25' reports that are true
src: It follows therefore that out of every 10 times that he names 25 he is right 9 times

lenses.title: §19. Two witnesses who both say 'white'
lenses.why: Combination of testimony, counted the same way: agreement helps, but only by a factor of about eight here.
src: Let us suppose two witnesses, the veracity of each being 9/10.

tree.label: drawings
src: out of 100,000 drawings (the number required in order to obtain a complete cycle of all possible occurrences, as well as of all possible reports about them)

children.label: both say white: right
src: the two witnesses agree in a correct report of the appearance of white in 81

children.label: both say white: wrong
src: and agree in a wrong report of it in 999.

answer.label: Share of their joint 'white' reports that are true
src: The Probability therefore of the story when so attested is 81/1080

lenses.title: Venn's footnotes, recomputed
lenses.why: Footnote 3 gives the general formula; three other printed results can be checked against it.
src: The generalized algebraical form of this result is as follows.

steps.label: Fn. 3: px / (px + (1−p)(1−x)), with p = 1/N
src: if he asserts that the event happened, the probability that it really did happen is px/(px + (1 - p)(1 - x))

steps.label: §10: a witness of veracity one-half leaves the odds unchanged
src: we find on calculation that his testimony goes for absolutely nothing; the chances that we have got the prize are just the same as they would be if he had never opened his lips, viz. 1/1000.

steps.label: §19: two concurring witnesses, black and white balls
src: The Probability therefore of the story when so attested is 81/1080

steps.label: §19: how much likelier than with one witness
src: makes the report nearly 9 times as likely as when it rested upon the authority of only one of them.

steps.label: §20: two concurring witnesses, numbered balls
src: The odds in favour of the event in fact now become 80919/80920, which are enormously greater than when there was only one witness.

steps.label: Fn. 7: digits in the denominator of Laplace's hundred dice
src: But the chance of this occurrence is represented by a fraction whose numerator is 1, and denominator contains 77 figures
steps.note: 100 fair dice showing one face: 1/6^99 (any face) or 1/6^100 (a named face). Both denominators have 78 digits. Venn may have read the base-10 logarithm, about 77, as the number of figures.

plot.caption: P(white | one witness says white) and P(white | two agree), against veracity, for a bag of N balls.

lenses.title: What Venn concludes
lenses.why: The chapter's real work is criticism: when the urn model applies, and when it does not.

cards.claim: The bags-and-balls method seldom yields numbers of practical value: we cannot say how often the event fails to happen.
src: It appears to me therefore that numerical results of any practical value can seldom, if ever, be looked for from this method of procedure.

examples.label: A trusted friend says something is to my advantage
src: Suppose that a person whom I have long known, and of whose measure of veracity and judgment I may be supposed therefore to have acquired some knowledge, informs me that there is something to my advantage

cards.claim: A witness's 'figure of veracity' depends on the kind of answer asked of him: yes/no or open.
src: the figure of veracity, or fraction representing the general truthfulness of a witness, is in a way relative, not absolute

examples.label: Yes or no: anyone can be right half the time
src: In a case of _yes_ or _no_, any one can be right every other time, but it is different where truth is single and error is manifold.

cards.claim: Rules for a 'contest of opposite improbabilities', such as Hume's deduction, have no general philosophical value.
src: It does not appear to me that the slightest philosophical value can be attached to any such rules as these.

examples.label: Hume: deduct one probability from the other
src: Hume, for instance, speaks of our _deducting_ one probability from the other, and apportioning our belief to the remainder.

examples.label: Thomson: one probability supersedes the other
src: Thomson, in his _Laws of Thought_, speaks of one probability as entirely superseding the other.

cards.claim: 'Extraordinary' has two senses: rare (a matter for probability) and evidence-resisting (a matter for the wider science of evidence).
src: there is considerable ambiguity and consequent confusion about the use of the term 'an extraordinary story.'

examples.label: The second sense
src: it is rather one which possesses, so to say, an actual evidence-resisting power.

cards.claim: Miracles cannot be modelled as rare draws, because their opponents deny that they ever occur.
src: How can any arrangement of bags and balls, or other mechanical or numerical illustrations of unlikely events, be admitted as fairly illustrative of miraculous occurrences

cards.claim: Without collusion, agreement on detailed accounts adds enormously; but collusion can never be calculated.
src: Practically our main source of error and suspicion is in the possible existence of some kind of collusion.

cards.claim: A defensible default: trust a witness's general veracity for ordinary and extraordinary stories alike.
src: it really seems to me that there is something to be said in favour of the simple plan of trusting in all cases alike to the witness' general veracity.

cards.claim: Disputes about miracles stall because the two sides differ on ultimate principles: universal causation or a superintending Providence.
src: a difference which reaches to ultimate principles is fatal to all argument.

examples.label: Shovelling in snow to dam a river
src: is like trying to make a dam, in order to stop the flow of a river, by shovelling in snow.

lenses.title: Venn's test cases
lenses.why: Each case presses on a general rule about extraordinary stories.

cases.rule: Extraordinary stories are less trustworthy than ordinary ones.
ruleSrc: That extraordinary stories are in many cases, probably in a great majority of cases, less trustworthy than others must be fully admitted.
cases.case: A naturalist reporting a monstrosity is believed almost as readily as when he reports something common, because he is more careful with the unusual.
src: Most persons, we may presume, would receive the statement of the naturalist in this latter case almost as readily as in the former

cases.rule: A witness trusted in ordinary matters can be trusted in each particular report.
ruleSrc: I have a gardener whom I trust as to all ordinary matters of fact.
cases.case: He says the dog has gone mad. Most reports of madness are really fits, so the report deserves doubt.
src: He tells me however that the dog has gone mad. Surely I should accept the statement with much hesitation

cases.rule: A witness of veracity one-half might seem to count for something.
ruleSrc: This is the case of a witness whose veracity is just one-half
cases.case: On a yes-or-no question he is just a guesser, and his testimony leaves the odds exactly where they were.
src: for this is really nothing else than the case of a person confidently answering a question about a subject-matter of which he knows nothing

cases.rule: The credibility of a story can be settled from the credibility of its witness.
ruleSrc: in which it is attempted to decide the matter simply by considerations about the validity of testimony
cases.case: A sailor finds stones laid out as a cross on a remote Pacific island. Whether the island has inhabitants decides the matter, not his veracity.
src: A sailor reports that in some remote coral island of the Pacific, on which he had landed by himself, he had found a number of stones on the beach disposed in the exact form of a cross.

lenses.title: Venn's terms
lenses.why: Venn coins two terms that map onto modern diagnostic-test vocabulary.

terms.period: The proportion of a witness's statements that are true, in the long run.
src: a witness who, on the whole and in the long run, is right in what he says nine times out of ten.

terms.period: His veracity for statements of one particular kind.
terms.modern: Positive predictive value: P(true | he says so).

terms.period: The fraction representing a witness's general truthfulness.
